posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: Previously I had great trouble with sticking gelatin to glass by silane'ing the glass with a solution of silane+acetone. I have found a new formula (from Bjelkhagens book) that seems to work much better for me. A mix is made with 40% silane + 45% Isopropylalcohol + 5% water. After 24 hours, this mix is further diluted with Isopropylalcohol to 5%. Then rub the glass thouroughly with this liquid and let it rest for about two hours. I then cleaned the glass further with glassex before application of the gelatin.

posts.author: semb
posts.content_md:
In the second step (dilution after 24h) do you mean diluted 1:20 with IPA at this stage, or diluted so the silane ends up as 5%?

Can this solution be mixed up and kept, or does it need to be used at once?

Simon

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: I always take 1cc of this solution and then add 19cc of IPA. The diluted solution can be used for about two days. Just rub it on a plate with a towel. You will see a white haze on the plate. I then put the plate away for a couple of hours and clean with a ammonia based glass cleaner. If you wait more than a day before cleaning the plate with glass cleaner, the white haze becomes very difficult to remove.

posts.author: semb
posts.content_md: Thanks for the tip. A few more questions - Should the solution only be applied to one side of the glass, or is it OK if it gets on the other side too? Is it important to apply it evenly all over? How should the diluted solution be handled - nitrile/neoprene gloves required?

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> Should the solution only be applied to one side of the glass, or is it OK if it gets on the other side too?

It's ok to apply on both sides. That way you don't have to remember what side of the glass will be the gelatin side. But because it is difficult to remove all visible traces of the white foggy precipitate, it is likely better to coat only the side that will contain the gelatin only. Also, if you apply only the side that is to be coated, any gelatin that inadvertently gets on the wrong side or on the edges can be more easily removed afterwards. It might even be a better idea (although I have not tried that yet) to treat the rest of the plate (especially the edges) with Rain-X. 

> Is it important to apply it evenly all over?

No, I just rub it on and let it dry.

> How should the diluted solution be handled - nitrile/neoprene gloves required?

I have been using kitchen gloves. I also use goggles and a painter's mask with carbon filters. The undiluted Silane is nasty stuff. You don't want to get that on your skin or breathe it. Mix it in a fume cuboard if you can. I mix it always outside the house.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Ok, not to take away from the subject but....

I have two heater/stirrers. One is pretty heavy duty and I am not happy with it because I can not set the temp to 115F. So one day I turn it on to cook some DCG and got called out of the room. I came back and the room was not smokey but smelled terrible. I cooked the AmDi gelatin to a nice hard black. I finally had to bust the beaker to get the magnet out. Boy that stuff stunk so bad it was day of airing out the lab to get back to normal. When I went in the lab, after I realized what happened, it was like.... I held my breath and ran in and opened a window. Then ran out and gasped for air. Then held my breath again and ran in an opened the door. The ran out and gasped for air. Then ran in again and put a fan in the door and ran out again gasping for air. My wife though I had completely lost it. But after smelling that stuff in the air once, I concluded, humans should not breath it. Not sure how toxic AmDi gelain is when it is cooked to a smoking boil but I didn't want to take any chances. I rarely use that heater/stirrer any more.

BTW, for a christmas presant a couple of years ago my wife went to a uniform company and bought me a white lab coat embrordered with the words "The Holographer" over the pocket. I love it and use it whenever I mix or clean and am using any chemicals. It really saves clothes.
